summary.text:
The paper set is a covering report (145233, 5 pages) whose figures all sit in the companion outturn report (145234, 34 pages). Read together. The cover report's unique contribution is on page 3: named authors with published emails — Oliver Colbert, Financial and Treasury Accountant, and Sandra Beard, Head of Finance. That is what unblocks the existing 'drafted-needs-address' pipeline state for Huntingdonshire.

Huntingdonshire is a net investor — £71.69m of investments against £34.25m of borrowing — and yet its financing cost ratio is already 15% of net revenue and its own budget takes it to 18% by 2027/28. The reason is definitional: the indicator counts MRP and PWLB interest paid without netting off the interest received, against a net revenue stream of only £25.6m.

Their own framing is the striking part: "The Authority is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget." Net investment income was £2.781m against gross service expenditure of £88.585m, and the budget needs it to rise to £3.755m. Meanwhile the treasury return fell from 4.45% to 3.75% in a year, with £46.3m of £69.7m sitting in the DMADF at 3.70%.

The borrowing side is the mirror image — five PWLB loans, nothing maturing for eleven years, three of them at 2.18% to 2.78%. Our file ties to their £34.255m at a weighted 2.84% and the maturity table rebuilds to 71%/29% exactly. On today's curve all five price below par, about £8.4m in total.

courses_named: PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator
officer.body:
Hi Sandra,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Cabinet on 14 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and it came out well. We hold five PWLB loans for Huntingdonshire totalling £34,254,685 at a weighted 2.84%, against the £34.255m average gross borrowing position and the 2.84% weighted rate in Section 6. Your maturity table rebuilds from the same five: the three loans maturing 2037 to 2039 are 70.81% of the book against your 71%, and the two running to 2057 and 2058 are 29.19% against your 29%. So we are certainly looking at the same book.

The thing that struck us is a combination we do not often see. You are a net investor — £71.689m of investments against £34.25m of borrowing, £37.44m net — and yet the financing cost ratio is 15% of net revenue and your own budget takes it to 18% by 2027/28. The arithmetic is right; it is the definition that produces it. The indicator counts MRP and PWLB interest paid and does not net off the interest received, against a net revenue stream of only £25.6m. Worth knowing when the number goes in front of members next to other councils', because a lot of authorities compute the same indicator net and the two are not comparable.

The sentence we would flag is your own: "The Authority is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget." Net investment income was £2.781m in 2025/26 and the budget needs £3.755m next year and about the same after. Against that, the treasury return fell from 4.45% to 3.75% in a single year, and £46.300m of the £69.703m sits in the DMADF at 3.70%. The DMADF is the safest place in the market and there is a perfectly good reason to be there — but it is also the lowest-yielding, and if the budget depends on investment income rising while the largest holding is in the lowest-paying instrument, the gap has to come from somewhere.

That is where we might genuinely be useful, and it connects to something else in your report: the investing limit with other local authorities was raised from £4m to £20m for 2026/27. Inter-authority lending is the market that sits between DMADF safety and credit risk, and it is the one nobody publishes. Every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution. We track it across the sector, so what other authorities are actually paying for one-month, three-month and six-month money is visible rather than inferred. For scale on the borrowing side, July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin markets are exactly when deposit rates get interesting. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On the borrowing side there is nothing to do and we are not suggesting otherwise. Nothing matures for eleven years, three of the five loans are between 2.18% and 2.78%, and on the DMO's premature repayment curve today the whole book prices about £8.4m below par. Standard caveats: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

One small note, offered because we would want to know. Your CFR appears as £74.682m in the indicator table and as a £75.682m closing balance in the movement table. A £1m difference with no explanation between them. It changes nothing material and it is very likely presentational, but if either figure gets quoted externally it is worth knowing there are two.

On training, four fit Huntingdonshire. DMADF deep dive and Money Market Funds (CNAV / LVNAV / VNAV) go to where the £69.7m actually sits. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is the one that matches the new £20m limit. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26 (cover report and outturn report), Cabinet, 14 July 2026.
